blocks.x: I'll make a note on here that we're interviewing Mr. Batiste Mosley at his home. What is the address? 1334 Pacific. 1334 Pacific in Algiers. And the date is September the 23rd, 1961. And I'll mention Ralph Collins is also here and this is Bill Russell. Do you mind giving your full name? Yeah, my name is John B. Mosley. John B.
Yeah.

And they call you Bat, of course. My familiar name is Batiste. How is that Batiste spelled? B-A-T-I-S-T-E. Can you tell us just when you were born and what part of town? I was born in 1893. Algea, Louisiana. Right here in Algea? Yeah. What was the exact birthday?
22nd of December. December. Pretty close to Christmas. Yeah, three days off.
Whereabouts in Algea were you born?
I was born right down the low coast here, where the Naval Station is now. September that night, that's where I was born at.
Oh, yeah. They always call you Bat?
Oh, that's my familiar name. That's my familiar name, Batiste. All the musicians, that's my familiar name, Batiste.

Yeah. I knew your brother before I knew you. Is he younger? I forget now. He's younger than I am. I thought he was younger than you. Yeah. Yeah, he's, I taught him drum. Well, they started at the beginning, could you tell us anything about your parents?
Did they play any music? No.
My father used to play.

What did he play? He used to play guitar. Oh, guitar. Yeah. And he's the one who started me out on drums from a little kid. Did he play in any band? No, he didn't play in no band by himself. He started out with a snare drum. I and him used to go out playing guitar and snare drum together. Oh, yeah? Yeah. We used to accumulate money like that, you know? Oh, yeah. And that started me on playing drums.
Was it a real snare drum? Yeah, it was a real snare drum.

He bought me. How old were you about when you did that? Oh, when I did that, I was about, oh, about nine years of age. Nine? Yeah, my father been dead about forty-some, forty-three years now. How old was he when he died? My father, when he died, he was only forty-one years of age. Not old at all. No. I didn't fool with drums until I got around about thirty years of age. And you really? And I really picked it up, yeah.
But what happened then between the time when you played with your father? Well. Didn't you play the drums then?
I just, only time I played with him, just iron him together.
Just around here.

And after he passed away, well, I just let it go, you know? Oh, yeah? And around in the thirties, the boys started to worry me again, well, pick up drums and try to learn them. So I picked them up and I started playing.

Well, when you played with your father, did you play for parties? Yeah, we played for parties, yeah, during that time. They called penny parties. Oh, yeah? Yeah, we used to play during that time, for penny parties. Did you play with anybody else at all besides him?
Well, after he passed away, we had what you call, we used to call them field bands.
Oh, yeah.

Oh, yeah. Yeah, the marches. Yeah, the marches. Yeah, the piccolo and a bass drum and a snare drum. Yeah. Just like the Army, you know, something like that. Yeah. Like the vipen drum bars. Yeah, that's it. And we used to play at parties like that. We used to play street, too. Used to call what you call the old grand armies. Used to town out every year, go to Chalmette. Yeah. And we used to play, used to have old Smoke and Mirror, used to run down there during that time.
Yeah, yeah. And we used to play for them.
Yeah, that's right. We used to play for them every year. Yeah. How many were in that field band? You only had three of us, a piccolo, a bass drum, and a snare drum.
Who played with you there?
That was, he's dead, and a fella called Jack, used to call him Jack Paeda. On the piccolo?
On the piccolo, yeah.

Uh-huh. And I was on the bass drum, and another fella called, let's see what his name was. Oh yeah, called him, uh, Albert Silvey. He was playing, you know, you know, they're dead now, they've been dead for many years. I was real young before they died, when they died. And that's why we continued. Finally, we made up a little, an orchestra, you know, six piece. Yeah. And, uh, this fella, what, I call you Jack Paeda, what they call him, he was playing trumpet, and they had me playing snare drum, I mean, trap drum. The whole set. They had another fella called, uh, Julius Gronison, he was playing bass. And another fella, Ernest, Ernest, uh, Silvey, he was playing clarinet. And, uh, another fella, yeah, what they call him, all I know his name was Booz Silvey, he was playing, uh, guitar. And that's, he had six pieces. That bass was a string bass? It was a string bass during that time, yeah. And, and, and, from now to, well, after they passed away I gave it up, and, uh, around the 30s I picked it up and started playing it.
Well, how old were you when you gave it up then, that first time?
Oh, when that first time I get up I was around, oh, about, oh, about 16 years old.
Oh, you were still quite young when you were. Yeah, still quite young, yeah.
Especially that kind of music, you know. Yeah. After the old fellas, they passed away, and some other way, and all, well, I decided to stop.
What kind of pieces did they play?
Did they play regular marches, or what? Well, they played regular marches, a lot of Dixieland stuff too, we used to play for parties, you know.
Dance music?
Dance music, yeah, we used to play dance music. Waltzes?
Waltzes, waltzes.
Were they still playing? Oh, that time, waltzes, and the Hurt Getson, and the Chattis, and during that time, we used to play those kinds. It was real Dixieland it was that time.
That was with the dance band? That was the dance band, yeah.
Well, I was thinking of the little, uh, trio.
You know the three piece band?

Oh, we would play march music. Yeah. Most was street playing, you know. Yeah. He had a, what they called the old Grand Army, the old Civil War fellas there, they all would live in that one. We used to go to Chalamet every year, and we used to play for them. A lot of time they'd have a parade around here, we'd play three pieces.
Well, when you went to Chalamet, what did you do? Take Smokey Mary?
That's right, take Smokey Mary, take you out there.
So, right down to the Chalamet, please?
That's right. Smokey Mary used to go down there. Oh, I did. And otherwise, if you wouldn't take that, you'd have a boat used to run down there.
Oh.
One of those side wheel boats? Yeah. They used to run down there with people and take them down there.
Did you play on the boat?

I played on the boat too, yeah. I forget the name of the boat, but I played on two side wheels. Oh, yeah. One of those old times. But they used to take you down there too. Then I used to play out in Bucktown.
Yeah?
Yeah. Played in.
Parading out there?
No, used to play in, for those, in those camps, you know, for dance, clubs, you know. Yeah. Used to get dancers out there.
What was that, for White College? For White.
For White. Yeah. We used to play out there pretty often in Bucktown. But there's nothing to it in them all up there, no? No, just not much?
No. That was your little six piece band you were talking about?

That was a six piece band during that time. Well, during that time, that's the most they was using, six pieces, during that time. Then I played with, later on I played with Poissy Humphrey. He had a big band.

I was going to ask you, before you got that far, about your drum set, when you started, when you were young, still just a boy, I guess. What kind of a drum set did you have? You had your old snare. Yeah. We had old snares.

We had bass drums. They had rope on them. I guess you done seen those. I've seen rounds of kids too, yeah. They have little rubber things like on them. You'd pull them, you'd grease them as rosim, you know, and you'd pull them down, that would tighten it. Yeah.
They wouldn't slip back?

They wouldn't slip back because you'd grease past that rosim over the rope part, you see? Yeah. And they had little hooks on it. Every hook that he attached to the drum. And you'd pull that little piece down like that, and that would hold because you'd grease them as rosim, you see? And the snare drum I had during that time, this had one head.
Oh yeah?

Yeah. Just about a head. The snare drum? Yeah, the snare head, yeah. No bad. And how they had the snares was underneath that one, that head, that single head. Yeah, the snare head. Because I'd underneath that another part was open. Yeah. That's how we started.
Was there any difference in the sound of this?

Oh yeah, during that time. We didn't have more than snares like we have now, you know? It was something like a cap gut string, something like that. Oh yeah. It's like you'd put on violin a long time ago. Kind of red? Kind of red, that's right, that's where they were. Yeah, I see. And the bass drum there, it had those ropes like I see on there. Oh. And had those catches on there. You'd grease it with rosim, then you'd pull it down and it would hold it like that. Yeah.
What else did you have?
Well, we only had cymbals. That's all cymbals and snare drum and that bass drum.
Any wood blocks or cowbells or anything like that? Well, not during that time.

But after I started playing with Poison M. Umphrey, well him and the old man Umphrey, well they had a ten piece band. Well I had all that jungle. I had cowbells, coconut blocks. Is that a dance band? Yeah, it was a big dance band. Yeah, big dance band. Yeah, big dance band.
Well, was that still before you'd quit when you were sixteen? Oh no, that was way after that.
I thought I taught in the thirties then. In the thirties, yeah. I started with him.
Would that be old Jim Humphrey, the professor? They used to call professor. Well, he was professor.
He was here.

Or was it Willie? Willie, the old man Willie. That was his son, Willie. Yeah, the old man Willie played clarinet, understand? Clarinet and saxophone. Used to be a truck driver or at least drive murals. For himself, yeah, he had teams for himself. Was it his band or his father's band? Well, that was his band during that time.
The fourth half was on, because the fourth half got too old, you know. But they had him and his son called Poissy.
Yeah, we know.
He was playing trumpet. And the old man was playing saxophone and clannery.
We met him too, remember? We went up to the festival.

Yeah, he's in the horn now. Oh, he is? Yeah. He had his legs amputated, I think. Yeah, that's right. Well, during that time we had ten pieces then. Well, that's the time I got, I had everything to go with the drum then. I had zillophone. I had to learn how to read. I didn't spend a nickel for reading, but the fellas playing bass was in Joe Howard. I guess you heard of him.
Oh, yeah, I heard of him.

Well, he'd teach me how to play drum music. Oh, yeah. And he tried to play those zillival and all. And after I got through it, well, I had everything to go with the drum. I had a bucket I'd taken and put cow skin on it and had a rope on it. Oh, yeah. That was a tiger when you played tiger rag. We used to use a thing like that for Halloween. Yeah. We used to use a tin can and the rope and the rods and the rods and the rods. Yeah. I had a bucket, a galvanized bucket, and I put a caja on top of it. And at the bottom there I had that rope tied in there. And I'd rise them at it, you know. When we played tiger rag, I had it hanging up on the stand. When we played tiger rag, I just pulled on it. And I'd start to tie it.
And say, the tiger's roar.
Yeah. And I had everything to go with drum. Boat, whistle, tram whistle. Everything that consumed, you know, for drums during that time.
Well, when was it you started to teach your brother Edgar?
I started teaching him around in, oh, must have been around in 34. Oh, yeah.
Yeah. He hadn't played before that? He hadn't.

He was, you know, just fooling around, but I didn't teach him. Then I started him out playing, showed him how to use it. And finally I'd take him in the street van. He used to play with me in the street van. I showed him how to play bass drum. What street van was that? That was, uh, they call, uh, the Tuxedo.
Oh, the Young Tuxedo? The original Tuxedo.

Oh, the original. Yeah. See, after Silver Stagg gave it up, uh, the old man Eddie Jackson, I'll get your head up with him. The Cuba play, I've heard. That's right. He was the manager of the band, and I was the assistant manager. Yeah. Well, he'd take it all over.
Eddie Jackson lived over on this side of the river. That's right. That's right. He lived here on Monroe Street.
That's why he died from me. He gave me that Tuxedo, that tuba, and I didn't want it. I sold it to a fellow, you know, and gave his wife.
Well, you got us too by then.
Yeah, but I did away with it.

I remember a couple of years ago, somebody had heard he left the string base too. Do you know if he had one? No, no, he did away with that before he died. No, because if he'd had that, I'd had that too. Yeah, somebody was out of that. But I was really nice to him, you know. You know about when he died, what year?
When he died? Yeah, he died around 1938. 1938. That's right. About the time I started coming back.
Yeah, during the present time. Now, how old was he? Middle age or old age? When Eddie died, he was about 71 or 72 years of age. Oh, really old. Oh, yeah, that's right. Yeah, he'd been there.

He was an old-time musician. Yeah, must have been there. He used to play, he was managing the tuxedo band when Celestine was running. Yeah, and he died around 71 or 72 years of age. Because I used to go see him all the time.
Well, I think of it, I never even got to meet Henry Allen, Sr., the old man. The old man? Well, he died.
He lived about up here, not far from here. Well, he lived right around here on the canal here. That's where he died. Right down here. Right around the corner here on the canal.
What street is that?
That's Lamarck Street.
Lamarck?

Yeah. That's in, let's see, how far, that's in the 600th block. Not this block, not that and the next one. Used to be a canal that year, but it's Philly now, it's a street now, you see? Well, it's on property, it's right there now. Did you ever play in his band?
Yeah, I played with Allen too. Well, you played with all the groups over there? Yeah, I played with him.
Snap drum, half time, bass drum. I played with Philly all the old times.

Who else was in Henry Allen's band when you played with him, do you remember? Well, they had his brother, I used to play bass drum, had his brother, George Allen. He was playing snap. When your brother played?
Yeah. Is he younger than the old man Henry? He's dead too now. Is he still living? No, he's dead too.
Oh, he's dead.
Yeah. Well, all the brothers are dead now.
Those are the two brothers playing.

I think so, he's always dead too. Yeah, they're dead now. Well, during that time, he had an 11-piece band, you know? Yeah. But pretty much all the old fellas, they passed away now. Who else played trumpet in it, do you remember?
Who else, besides Henry Allen?

Well, they had a son playing it sometime? Well, his son played sometime when he was here. That's before he left here. Before he left. Yeah, he played. Then they had a fella called Wooden Joe. Oh, yeah. He used to play with him. Then they had a, well, this fella, a young fella, when he came along, Alvin Alcorn, he played with him. And they had, let's see who it is. Well, Poison, or Willie Alfre, he played with him too. Clarinet. Yeah, he played Clarinet. Yeah. During that time, they only used Clarinet in the band then. They didn't use no sight. And they had old man, Bob Rand. Oh, yes. He played alto. Yeah. And we had a fella, he's from Baton Rouge, he left here. He was playing bass. He had one of those, you know, upright basses. Upright basses? Yeah. A little short fella. He was, he's in California now. I used to call him Bassie, that's all I know. What does he name? Bassie. He was that short fella, yeah. He left here and went to California out there. Well, he was playing bass. Do you remember who was on the bass? Then they had Harrison Bond. Oh, yeah. Trambone? He's dead now. Yeah. Had him on the trambone. Nine years ago. Yeah. He's been dead now. Oh, but pretty near two years now. Has he been that long? Yeah, pretty near two years he's dead. Had him on the trambone. And they had that old fella there called Jack Carey. He's dead.
You heard of him?
Oh, we haven't heard a lot about him. Yeah. Well, he's dead now.
I was about the youngest. I was about the youngest.

in the band during that time. Do you remember who was playing baritone horn? Baritone horn? They had a fella called Frank. Frank Joseph, he was playing, he's dead now. Yeah, he was a cook, he used to cook on the clubs out there. He used to cook on what? He used to cook on one of those boats out there on the river. Oh yeah? Yeah. He was a little short fella. He had one of those upright bass. I mean a valet horn, yeah. Then finally after he passed away too. Late, before Mount Allen died he had a, this fella he's dead now. John, I forget his name. Living on the oldest kid. I can't think of last night. He was playing.

You remember when you were a boy, the real old band Professor Moneta tells about his brother, Norm, was it his brother? Yeah. Or his uncle. His uncle had a brass band way back. That would be when you were. No, I don't know. See, he's

way older than what I am, you know. Yeah, he's. I don't remember. It was Pacific brass band. Oh, the Pacific, yeah, I remember that. Remember Pacific? Oh yeah, I remember that. That's way back, isn't it? That's way back. I was nothing but a young kid then. Uh-huh. I used to go around listening to that. On that street called the Almas Street. It was in the four, five, in the six on the block. About there. The Almas? The Almas, yeah. They used to rehearse for that. The fella used to have been in a band. He used to, uh, Sims. Old man Sims. George Sims. Oh yeah? Yeah, he was the manager of the band. And that's, uh, I remember one old fella used to play bass drum in there. I don't know his first name was George. He used to live your analogies too. He's been dating now for about, oh, he's been dating now for about

10, 11 years. I wonder why they called it Pacific. This is Pacific Street, isn't it? Yeah, yeah. Well, that's the old Pacific band. During that time they had the Pacific, there wasn't no such thing as a Tuxedo band. It wasn't existing. Is there any Pacific railroad or anything here that they might? Well, they had the Southern Pacific right back here, you know. Pacific right back here.

Yeah, Southern Pacific. Used to be the shop right there. Maybe that's it. Maybe that's what they called it, yeah. They had that band. They had the Golden Leaf band. They had about two or three of them around here. Well, the Tuxedo band wasn't in existing during that time. Oh, before that time. Yeah, that was in Miami. The Excelsior band. Excelsior band I was in. Well, Peter Boccage was in that band.
Was their headquarters mostly over here on this side or the other side of the river?

Well, the biggest majority of them was from New Orleans. The only one they had in the Excelsior band was Peter Boccage and another fella. He's dead now. I forget his name too. He's been dead now for about 13 or 14 years. Did they ever have such a thing as a Pickwick band over here? Had a Pickwick band? Not over here. No, I've heard of them over here somewhere. They had it in New Orleans.
Oh, they did? Yeah, Pickwick band. It was in New Orleans. Was it a brass band?

It was a brass band, yeah. Well, you know, during that time they played street music and dance music too. That was old band. Yeah. That's the time they used to all have a uniform made, you know. That's the time the band would come out. They'd always be, well, it was an organized band during that time. Whenever you see a band out, they were the same faces all the time. It's not like here. Every time you see a street band out, there's different faces. Yeah. But during that time, they was organized. They'd rehearse around two and three times a week. Yeah. Yeah.
Well, they'd play a lot from music, wouldn't they?
Oh, strictly music.
Strictly from music.
Yeah, what you call the Red Book during that time. Yeah. They all had nothing but cornets then. No such a thing as no trumpet. Well, they had a real,

real street band. What did they play? For instance, at a funeral, did they play any hymns? Yeah, they played hymns. All that music. They wouldn't make the music for some time? Well, there was particularly music. They'd use that music. It was fun. Like, say, they play, well, for instance, like now they play the saints, the walks, the walk, and all those. Yeah. But did they have any spirituals or any hymns in those days that they used much?
The most they used. Like By and By or anything? Well, they played that. That's old, you see. Glory land? Yeah, that's old. These hymns like by head, you know.
That's what I was going to say. All those hymns, they didn't need the music for that?

They didn't need the music for that, no. But like anything like that number 134, number 19, all I get, we had the music to play. It was complicated. But like all those old hymns you mentioned there, why they didn't even play it by head. Yeah. Well, they'd have all that memorized.
Oh, they'd have all that memorized, yeah.

So coming back from... And if they wouldn't, the fellas that'd get in the band wouldn't have it memorized, they'd write it for you, you see, so you don't understand it, yeah. Now you take some fellas right now, they can't play a piece of music if they don't have music. Even the blues, they got to write it for them. They're just accustomed to that. Now Peter Burkhardt had a son there. He could play nice, Edwin Burkhardt, but he couldn't play a thing if he didn't have the music. He wanted to write everything,

blues and everything else for him to play. Otherwise, he couldn't do anything. Was running on the way back, say from the funeral, like when they have, didn't they ramble and some of the... Well, they played out, yeah. They played ramble. Did they know any of the other jazz tunes or Dixieland, what they call Dixieland tunes? Yeah, they knew all the head numbers like that. They had those head numbers.

Yeah, they had them like that. Yeah, they played out. So like them. They knew ramble and different things like that. All those old numbers like that. They wouldn't know them. So they didn't... You take the musicians during that time, well you take during that time outside playing street music like that, the fellas playing like dance music, didn't know anything but reading. You take like Jim Wright, now he played for you before I was playing, but he didn't know how to read. George Lewis, he was playing before I didn't know how to read, but you know, he had a good memory.
He had a good memory.

I see we used him in the tuxedo band, George, and we played him funeral march, and good memory he played, just like he was. But during that time, like I say, like dance music, that he didn't know anything with music. Yeah. Just all gin. A lot of times they'd make up different things, you know, call it the onion rags and all that kind of stuff like that.

Yeah, they'd make it up like that and play. That's the way it was. I wanted to ask something about the, something about the clubs over here. Yeah. How many different clubs can you, I know now there's the Wolves up in Gretna. Well during this time there's the Wolves, that's in Gretna, and they have the young men's. That's still here down on Homer's side.

Yeah, one down here, and then they have another young man up here. Oh, that's okay. That's the hall. Yeah, the young men's hall. That's still there. That's still there. Yeah. Well that's, the bands that, right now, well that's gone now. That's right the next, on the canal there. Used to be a canal there. Yeah.
Well they tore that down?

No, it's a resident now that people lived there. Oh. That's still there. Yeah. Well that used to be the, the society. Is it on the corner? Right on the corner. Used to be a society used to own that. But they call it a friend of Pearl Grace.
What is that, three story building?
No, it's just one.
Just one story.

You see like you go to the corner right here, when you get right to that corner, that you got grocery on this side and right across the street. That's the, that's the, that's the, that used to be the turtle bike.
Yeah, everyone, you want to take a picture of it. Yeah.
Yeah. It's all over there. It's the people living in there.
It's got the sort of a round roof.
It's tin. It's tin and all over there.
Yeah. Is that the same block where there's an Alps place or something?

Well the Alps place, yeah, but before you get to the Alps place, it's like go to the corner here. Yeah. You'll go right to that corner there on this side is the grocery and right across the street from there. That's the turtle bike.
Yeah, I think I know the one.
Yeah. Yeah.
You couldn't, one day I was telling you to get a photograph of it and it wasn't short. Yeah, that's it. That's the place.
That's the only thing. That used to be a dance hall?
That used to be a dance hall.
Maybe.
It used to be an open pavilion, you know.
Oh yeah?
Yeah.
It didn't have sides?

It didn't have sides. Just the roof? Just the roof, that's all. That's all. The branches all around. I wonder if it's lower than that. Yeah. So finally, the Banger, they bought the place and made it for dwelling place. People lived there. It used to belong to the Friends of Progress. It was an old society.
Friends of Progress.

Friends of Progress, yeah. Then that house hall right there, that used to be a an outfellow hall, that is. An outfellow hall. Yeah. Then you used to have that old hall down on Siglin Street, used to be the outfellow's hall, around Siglin and Evelina. Oh yeah. And that was all about that. Yeah. There used to be an old outfellow hall. That's torn down, isn't it? Oh yeah, there's nothing but a resident there. No. Well during that time, all those hall, you could get what they call the bonkets, you know. And they'd get a band, a string band to play there. Play there and get down.
When you say string band, what was the instruments on a string band?
Well that was six pieces. You take drum, bass, guitar, trumpet, clarinet, how many that, five, that's six, yeah. No piano, didn't know anything but no piano, nothing like that.
Did you have a trombone?

Yes, that's what it is, that's six pieces, trombone, yeah, that's six pieces. They call it a string band because of the bass and guitar? Yeah, that's what they call the string band, yeah. Didn't know anything but no piano during that time. Yeah. That's all. And they had those, just common guitars, you know. Yeah, without electric. Yeah, well they didn't know anything but electric, no. You couldn't hardly hear it the way it was. Well, it seemed like your string band. And after they started, they started on banjo, after the guitar went out of style. Well they found banjo, you know, it was better torn, no louder, you see. Well that's why they started, just making banjos. And that's what they used. They still had a six piece band then, when they had those banjos. That's what you called the real Dixieland band then, the six piece band.
But in the old days you called them a string band?

Called them a string band, that's right, in the old days. No orchestra, none of them, none of them was a string band. Folks like here lately, that's why people give them a damn of jazz, you know. But during that time it was a string band, six pieces, right and all, that's all they had, six pieces.
Well the music that they played, what did you call that, just dance music?
Just dance music, yeah, that's all. I told you like, it's called quadrille, shatters, waltz. I don't got to play that, you know. Yeah.

It's been so long that I knew the waltz. Well there's one other club I remember myself in, up with the bridge, is it the Eagle Eye? Eagle Eye, that's right, Eagle Eye, yeah. Whatever happened, I know they tore it down.

They tore it down, well it's still up now, but they don't use any more ban now. They don't use ban? No, the only one here in Algea is use a ban, that's the young men's right here. Well in Grettony, the young men's up there, you know what I'll tell you about, they use a ban, and the wolf.
The wolf, they use the...
They used to have another club up there, yes, back used to call the Lions, they used to use bands too. In Grettony? In Grettony, yeah, the Lions club, they used to use bands.
Well maybe you can speak me out too on the McDonaldville, where the people talk like it's a separate town. Where would you start, is it outside the city limits?

Yeah, you see after you pass under the bridge here? Yeah. Well after you pass under the bridge, that's Jefferson Powers. Yeah. And when you're coming back after you get from on this side of the bridge, that's New Orleans Powers. That's why Jefferson, of course you used to call it McDonnellville, now it's considered all Grettony now. It's really outside the New Orleans area.
That's right, that's right. Was it between Algiers and where Grettony used to be? Was it between those?

That's right, McDonnellville. I'll tell you how McDonnellville used to run from, this is what I tell you about the bridge. Yeah. Used to run as far as, like I tell you about the Young Man Hall up here. You know what I tell you on how it is. Yeah, that little hall. Yeah, well that was McDonnellville. And when it leave from there, going all the way around, it used to call that Grettony.
Did Grettony take all McDonnellville over?

That's all Grettony now. You don't call it McDonnellville no more. That's all Grettony. Right after you cross from under the bridge here, that's Jefferson Powers. That's all Grettony now. It's no more McDonnellville.
That's the deal for now. I was going to ask you about, you say you started teaching your brother when you came back in the 30s?
Around in 38.
Well, how did you teach him? I know you do those drum solos. Yeah. Who do you do it with now? You do it, Chester Jones?
Well, Chester Jones, he's the only one who can do it with me now since my brother gone. I've tried with them other fellas, you know, but they can't, I don't know, they're just all the same.
You were doing it a little bit the other day.

Yeah, the other day, the other week, yeah, yeah. But who was that? I think I could break him in if I was close around him, you know. Yeah, what's the name? Yeah, Booker T. Booker T. Yeah. Yeah, that's Booker T. Yeah. Well, I think if I was close around him, I could break him in, you know. Now, Chester, I broke him in on the drums.

Yeah, sounds very good. Yeah. You can almost, well, you can, you can sing the sound right on the drums. Yeah, that's right. Yeah. It's just like playing the melody. Yeah. Well, how do you do that? How do you teach anybody to do that?

Well, like he get on the bass drum, I get on the snare. And I just show him out of knife, he'd miss anything, well, I'll take the bass drum myself and show him the lick, you know, and the motion on it that way. But this fellow Booker T., I think if I was close around him, I could show him in. But the rest of the fellows, they're hard to catch on to.
Are you sort of singing the tune to yourself?

No, I don't sing at all. I just keep it in my mind. You keep it in your mind. Yeah. In, I take a solo like that too. With the, with the snare and the bass? That's right. You do all that. You do all that? I want to come down there one night. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I take a solo myself like that.
Yeah. Well, did you ever hear anybody else do anything like that?
That's the first, I'm all at one.
Yeah, I think so.
I've been all around. I've heard no one did it.
Did, did, did, did.

And I just picked it up. One Sunday we were playing, you know, we had a parade from, from down the low coast here come to Algevius. Right. And I had my brother with me. And I told him, I said, I'm going to try this, see if we can play it solo. He said, good. I think he can do it. He said, yeah, you don't like me, now I can do it. And we just picked it up. Yeah. Right on with it. Yeah. And after he left here, I got a chest and I broke him, you know. But the other fellas, I don't know, I just can't do it with them. I don't know, this fellas been playing so long, it seemed like they're going backwards to the front one. Yeah. That was a good one too.
Yeah. I can't understand them.

Now, I stayed off a drum, oh, about four or five years. I just thought, since everybody worried me, you know, playing snare, you know, street playing. And I'm just as good as I was before. Sure. It just ended. Yeah, that's right. Yeah, everybody's surprised, you know. But I figured what's in you, you know, it's just in you, that's all.
Did you keep your drums all that time?
Well, I got my snare here, but I got a boy, he used the rest of my drums. I keep my snare. See, and I got a little bass drum.
On one bass drum we saw that you played once, I mean you'd have gold and... That's my drum, that was my drum. The Golden Ruler on that. Yeah, that's mine. Golden Leaf. Golden Leaf.

Yeah, that's my drum. Golden Leaf. Yeah, but we had, after Tuxedo, we went out and Tuxedo existed, though, we made the band of Golden Leaf. You know, I was managing the band after Eddie died. So after he died, we changed, after John went to the Young Tuxedo, I changed my band to Golden Leaf. And I managed to tell him, some of the fellas passed away, so. I just quit fooling. And I let, uh, how... Oh, how...
I thought he kept my drum, finally did away with it now. I don't know where it's at.
I was going to ask you, did you ever hear of any of these bands, did they ever do any kind of a drum solo?
I never heard nothing of them do, I said.
You never did any kind of a drum solo? No.
I'm the only one. I never heard.
I think you're still the only one.
Yeah. It seemed like one day I heard Dave Bailey once, the little drummer of the band.

You know who was trying it once? I went, I saw him, they were playing a parade for a club, Jolly Bunch. He was a little short fellow, but he couldn't do it. It wouldn't be Abbey, would it? Abbey, yeah. And he had this same fellow playing bass drum with him, Booker T. Oh yeah. Yeah, yeah. They played for a club back at town there, the Jolly Bunch, they had a parade. I went back there to collect tax from them, and he tried it, but there was nothing to it.
Yeah, he heard me, you know.

You see, a lot of times when Howard was playing, he used to hire me, but for friendship he would take Abbey, you know, in the band with him too, and he'd cut off another man, see. Well, he used to be beside me, he used to let me play that solo like that. And he'd try and get that hang of it.
It really sounds very good. It should be recorded.

Well, I play in the orchestra the same way. They take down, I take that solo too. That's right. Yeah. I'm going to come down there one night there. If you would. They're all the warmen of death to come down there. I'm going to take that.
Howard has been playing there two and three. Yeah, they told me he's been playing that.
Oh, sometimes twice a week. Yeah, they told me that. He told me he'd get along pretty good.
He'd get along pretty excited.

Well, I'll tell you, as long as he keep off that stuff, you know. That's right, because he has to now after his operation and all that. Because the condition he was in there, he ought to keep off. He had partly lost his life. Yeah, almost. Yeah.
He very nearly died, I think.

Yeah, that's right. Because I used to see him pretty often. Go to the hospital and see him, you know. Yeah, I went a couple of times too. He got so bad. Yeah, he really did. So I haven't seen him in quite a while.
Yeah, he did. He looked like he's better now than I haven't seen him.
Oh, I was going to say, speaking of church, sorry I missed one of the Matthews brothers that played at church. Which one was that? Oh, yeah, he did. Yeah, Remus.
Remus Matthews, yeah. Well, he was a good friend of mine. Yeah. All of them used to play together. Where did they live?
Near this neighborhood? Never heard of him.

Well, he used to live right here on Bellwood Street. You ever passed that funeral home right there? Oh, yeah. My funeral home? Hello? Funeral home right there, right in the back of the funeral home is Bellwood Street. Well, he used to live right there. His wife is right there now. Oh, yeah? Yeah, she's right there.
Oh, maybe you've been dead or something.
Yeah, her name is Emma. Emma Matthews. Bebe, oh, he's been dead for years.
I never did know him.
Oh, he's been dead for years. Yeah. It's been a long time. First Bill we all know him.
Bill, yeah.
Well, he's the only brother. Yeah, he's the only one living in the house.
Yeah, yeah.
He's got several sisters like that. But Remus's wife, she's still in the same place yet. Right in the back of that mosque place. He said, that's Bellwood Street there. Bill.
Bill was playing his snares not too long ago.

Well, Bill was playing. That's the first sister we picked up. Drum. Yeah, he picked up drum. He used to play with a, oh, I forget the name of the band. I know the fellow who used to play trumpet. He was dead now. He was dead now. Lego. Lego? Lego, yeah. He was a good trumpet player too. That was old time. He had a beautiful tone. He had a beautiful tone. Well, he's dead now. Well, that's who he started out with. And finally, after he picked the, he started playing tram along with it. You heard about Punch. But he had not. But he started playing tram along with it when he got in Punch band. Punch had a six piece, a string band too, around here, for he left for me. He had a nice band too.

He could play too. Are there any of the other old time bands here that you can remember? For instance, they tell me about the Johnson brothers, Yank and the other. Yank, yeah. Yeah, it was Yank. There were two brothers. Both of them playing tram along. Buddy.

Buddy Johnson and Yank Johnson. And Frankie Dusen was over on the side. Frankie Dusen, yeah. Did you know that when they lived over here? I guess I did. He was playing tram along too. Yeah. He was a barber. He used to cut my hair. See where the Catholic cemetery right there? Yeah. That's the Catholic cemetery right opposite the Catholic cemetery. They were staying there. That's where the old man and all used to stay. Frankie Dusen, they call him. Frankie Dusen, his dad and all. You know his daddy played any instruments? No, his dad. He's not the one who played instruments. Frankie was the only one. Yeah. And he had another old fellow, your old bright fellow, used to play, old man, Darcy. He used to play bass. Oh, is that Eddie? He's still over there. He's still alive. Works for a bank and all? No, no. I know you talking about this old man, he's dead. Oh, that's right.
That was the man that the fast told us about. Cheese. Some joke about cheese. Yeah, he's fantastic.

He was that fellow. Very fair looking. Well, he used to play. And they had another musician over here, was one of the days. He used to play drums. Boynton II days. Well, he was playing with Frankie Dusen band during that time. Well, I remember them. Frankie Dusen, well he died in the city, he did.
Is there any kin of the Dusen still alive?
Well, he has some nephew here, but I don't know where. I think he has a daughter.
I think we heard about her. Yeah. She was living in Yaw, and that's who he was living with when he died.

Some daughter over there. Yeah, I think they were living around Genesis. Ron Jenner Street somewhere around there. Ron Jenner Ferret somewhere. I know that's why he died at Ron. I'm telling you, I know that's why he died, because I used to pass didn't talk with him. But that's all I know, Ron. All the other old people there passed away. But I knew them.

I remember Harrison Barnes told us about a few musicians. Yeah. Let's see, Hooker was one. Was he on this side of the river? The trumpet player was on the... What was his name? Hooker? Played the cornet, I think. Sounds like they might be Tom.
The only one I knew over there played trumpet was like Peter, the old timers. Not nothing of trumpet.
Where's Tom Albert? I guess came from this side of the river. Tom Albert. Yeah, he came.

Oh yeah, he came from down the low coast down there. I knew him when I was a kid. You knew him? Yeah, yeah. He was an old timers. Well I used to play with him. Oh you did? Yeah. You did too? Yeah, I used to play with him.
When you were still using that snare with one head? Still young.
Still young, yeah.
I used to play with him, nothing but a kid. So it was two days ago, I walked by, I was sitting there on the country street.

Then I used to play with him in the, in the ricka band. I played the ricka brass band. Yeah. I used to play with him in there. Old man, old carnish. Yeah. You remember him? Yeah. I never knew about him. And they had two Wilson brothers, one of them Wilson, he was, he run the band and the other one there was a ballotone player. Oh, when they ran the band, what did he play? Who that? The Wilson. Wilson, one played a trumpet, the other brother played a barotone. Barotone.
Yeah. Just yesterday we interviewed a drummer, Henry Robertson. Yeah. And they called Sleepy across the river. Sleepy, yeah.
Well I teach him drums.
He wait for another table. Oh yes. Yeah. I teach him. He was telling us. He told you. Yeah, he mentioned your name.
That's why we thought we'd better be talking to him. I could make a good drum out of him too.
But he won't get in the local, you see. He was in there. He was telling us about a man by the name of Wilson, that, wasn't that Wilson that plays the clarinet?
Yeah, he didn't know his first name.
He couldn't think of his first name. Do you know? He still plays. They have a non-union band that they work with.
That was a man in his seventies I guess he'd be.

Said he lived downtown. I don't think I've ever heard of him or know anything about him. He's a pretty good clarinetist. He never knew him. He might have the name wrong too. His memory wasn't too bad sometimes.
I know some of them Barnes, they don't want to play clarinet.
Yeah, Mealy Barnes, of course we know. He's old, he's old.
Yeah. He don't know, he's on union. I know him. And they had another colleague called Big Eye Louie. Yeah, I knew him.
He's dead now, I believe.
Yeah, he was a clarinet player.
When you played with Tom Albert in those old days, what was Tom playing then?
He was playing trumpet.
You were on the street, in the street?
He was playing in the street too.
Oh, you played in his orchestra too? Yeah. Played for dancing?
Yeah, I played for dancing with him too. Oh yeah?
Yeah.
What kind of... Most of his work used to be down in a place called Violet down there. Oh really? Well known, they used to trap his old people. And you used to get more of that work down there.
How did you get down there in those days?

Well, they used to go down there, he had an old car. Car, automobile, yeah. You told us about it, he used to play Delacro Island. Well that's what I'm talking about down there. Yeah, you see he used to go down there, he had a trap and he was all crazy about it. Only thing he'd have down there, he wouldn't get nobody down there but him.
Who'd they have in the family side of yourself?

Well they had me, they had him, and they had... I forget that fella, he's dead now. Let's see who is. I think he had five pieces in there down there. He didn't have no bass, I know that. Boy, I forget the fella's name, no I can't think... I know it was me, and that's how the fella, I can't think his name, he's dead now, he's looking up front of town.
What do you play?
What he's playing? He's playing? Yeah, what do you play? He's playing guitar. Yeah, I forget his name, it's so long. He's been dead. He's worked for a furniture store.
Did he have a bass drum too? No, he didn't have no bass. Just snare and guitar? Yeah, that's all.

And uh... They had, this is, they had guitar and trumpet. And they had uh... This old fella, yeah he's dead now, he's a play, clown there. Old uh... You see Fat Domino? I think it was his uncle, old man Baptiste. Oh yeah? Yeah, I can't think of his name, he was, he dead now. He's living right near my family, they had old sakes living there. Right in the middle of his name now. That's right. That's right. Were there any other bands around on this side of the river that stayed over here and never psychies live in there.
Were there any other bands around on this side of the river that stayed over here and never got across the river much as you can think of? Like I said, the Johnson, Buddy Johnson band that they

worked mostly in? Oh yeah, the most they played was in Yawlin. Well you take all the bands from that time, the most they played was in Yawlin. One time we played over here, one of those halls, you know society would give a dance, you see. I like to take like SP out there, used to pay off like twice a month, you see. Well every time the SP, because they had a lot of people waiting, every time they would pay off or they'd have a dance here. I had a place right there, Precious Ranch used to be right here, several blocks from here. Oh I heard. That was a dance pavilion. Well they used to give dances there, those bands used to play there. But the biggest majority of the Yawlin, you see, used to have what they called those caberets during that time. And most of the band used to play those caberets. And that was in Yawlin.

Fess of course, he's older than you and his memory goes back and forth. He told us about places over like on Brooklyn Street, the ping pong. Do you remember that old place? Yeah, and that's what they called the hunky-tonk.

Then they had another place out here on Wilmore in Brooklyn, with the green tree. That was called the hunky-tonk too. Then they had another place out here on Tash and Bringer, right by the bridge out there, right on evening. They had a place that was called the hunky-tonk. But I'll tell you, the most of those places used to have pianos, you know. Those old-time pianos, those rollers. Well they used that, you see. They couldn't afford, you know, green at that time and high bands. Most bands would play over here when society would give a dance, see.
When you say a roller, do you mean the mechanical piano?

Yeah, yeah, you remember those player pianos? That's what they used then. You'd put a quarter in them? Or what did he put in them? No, the fella just sit down there. During that time, after that, but the first time, when the first started, finally he saw him with his foot. The pedal it, see. It did give him a dollar a night. Oh, I see. That was big money then. He sat down there and pedal it. Finally, after the, you know, change like that, everybody started having those kind of put a nickel in it.
But you could play them with your hand?

You could play with your hand during that time too if you could play. Yeah. Just lift the top off, you know, and cut that foot off while you'd wake up. You'd pedal. You could play them with your hand too. And after that, they'd raise them with some kind of, you know, put a nickel in it and it'd be by itself. And before that time, you'd pedal it, you know. They'd give a fella a dollar a night. Well, we used to play every night for a dollar a night. Yeah. During the pressing time. Yeah, I guess so. Yeah. Well, good answer to that. Seven nights, seven dollars. Yeah. Big money then. Well, you'd make pretty good chips, you know. Yeah. That was Jitney during that time. They'd start those Jitney dances around there. Well, the Jitney dances, they'd start that, they'd give you fifteen dollars a week. Well, the Johnson Yankee and Buddy Johnson, these are played over. That's the most they did, played those Jitney dances. On the other side of the river. Yeah, but they had one place where the Yankees were playing right on the corner, working there in the canal, it was upstairs. That place there. Then they had the Budweiser, you know. Yeah, I was in there before they were there. Yeah, yeah, that. Then they had a place in Exchange Island instead too. Royal Foster now used to play in there.
You heard, you know.

We interviewed him. Yeah, yeah, he used to play in there. He loves drums. Yeah, he likes to play some drums. Yeah, yeah, he tried to play everything. He loves drums. But he never make a drummer. I tell you, you got a lot of them around here that never make it. Been playing the four hours. This fellow Rudolph, he played over there last Sunday. You saw him? Big Rudolph. You saw him last Sunday? Well, they wanted me to play, but after they had him, I can't play with them fellas. They asked me first, but I got that other fella, Bigfoot Bill, with him. I sent him on that job. But I can't play with them fellas, you know. They worry me. Mess me up. I thought he had Alfred, you see. I didn't build many kinds of it, because I played bass drum with Alfred. Yeah. But them other fellas, they didn't. Them the contraro too, you know. You see, playing music, you got to have a satisfied mind. Everybody be pleasant. But if any time you just satisfied like that, things ain't going to go right. You got to have a satisfied mind. And you got to have a mind. You got to have a satisfied mind. You got to have a mind.
That's all what you're doing. Otherwise, things ain't going to go right.
Well, what do you think the role of the drumming in the band is? I mean, what do you try to do to help the band when you drum?

Well, when I'm drumming like that, see what I do if a drummer like that, if you don't know, I'll try to talk to them, you know. And I'll take one stick, you know, like that, and try to show them when they hit. But some people come and try, they don't want to tell them nothing.
Well, what I'm trying to say is, what are you trying to do when you're drumming? You trying to keep a steady beat?

Oh, yeah, yeah, steady beat, yeah. Study beat. This is when the drummer beat my alarm, you mean? Yeah, either way. Well, you see, yeah, steady beat. Now, you see, you see your drumming, you see the drummer, that's the time in the band. You can take a drummer there, you fall down, you pick up, you throw everything out of time. But when you're playing drummer, like I play with a band like that, you got to have a steady time. You see, like you're playing a pune like that. You take a bass drummer like he didn't know how to tell him if I ain't playing bass drum. You always knock off on your left foot. If you knock on that right foot, you're going to throw everybody out of line, out of time. You're not watching, you're not hollering at everybody when I'm playing bass drum. On that left. And when you ever see everybody walk that left foot, put it on that left. You never go wrong that way. That's when you're playing bass drum? That's when you're playing bass drum, yeah. That's like that fellow I played with the other cymbal. I told him, I was telling him, I said, I never hit until you get everybody on their left foot. You know, everybody on their left foot you're watching. When you hit, then you hit on your bass drum. You'll never knock them out of time that way. It's always one, two, three, four. One, two, three, four.
What do you do? Hit the bass drum on one and the cymbal on two?

No, just like you hit on the left foot, boom. You like playing a few of them. You know, boom. You don't hit that cymbal. You see, when you're playing a few, you don't use that cymbal at all. No. That's right, they don't use that cymbal at all. I use that mouse. All you got to do when you hit on that foot, it's not about boom, boom, boom, boom. Now, when you're playing, you know, like, you're playing, you know, jazz piece, something like that, but you hit off with both cymbals like that.
Well, wait a minute. You say, you say, the drum and the cymbal together?
When you're playing, you know, a march piece like that. Yeah. But if you're playing a few of them, you don't use that cymbal at all. Just use that mouse. That's all.
Well, what are you doing right now?
You see, when you hit off, when you hit off on, bam, like that. Up and down. Then you go on.
Well, it seems like you're hitting the cymbal in between the bass drum.

Yeah, it's up and down. Yeah. It's half the beat on your cymbal all the time. Half the beat on the cymbal. On the cymbal all the time, yeah. It's just like when you're playing an orchestra, that sock cymbal, that's half the beat on that all the time, yeah. Because a lot of people get messed up with it, you know, because they're not accustomed to it. Yeah. But it just half the beat. Just foot foot and that neck. That's something. A lot of people.
I noticed about your role, too. You have quite a distinctive role.
Yeah, well I have all kind of role. Well, I studied all that, you know. Yeah. A lot of, now the important thing is that crushed roll I make. Plenty of people can't make that.
Well, what is that exactly, crushed roll?

It just started like that. Just throw the stick into your... That's all. Actually, you don't understand. Don't move your wrist. Just your fingers, that's all. Excuse your fingers. You ever notice, yeah, I don't move my wrist. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. People can't get that.

Yeah. Yeah. Right, you think. Some people call that a press roll. Yeah, because I'm all calling it a press roll. But in the book, it's a crushed roll. Press roll. Yeah. In the book, it's a crushed roll. Yeah. A lot of people call it a press roll.
Did you study all that stuff yourself?

I study all that myself. Yeah. Yeah, just come to me. I see the second time, the first time I played, I got with a band, with a Royal Jazz Band. Well, I played a fella, yeah, he's dead now. Lil Tramont player, Joe Harris. Yeah. He's dead now. That was his band. Let's see, they had me, they had a fella called Frank. Frank Jones, he dead. Joe Harris, he was dead. He was playing tramo. Then they had a fella, boy, he lived in, Harry Vinnett. He lived in St. Rose now. He was playing trumpet.
What was his name again? Frank Burnett.
V-I-N-E-T.
Yeah.

He was playing trumpet. He lived in, that's his home in St. Rose. He's back home now. And we played that Sunday night. We left here and went to Mobile that, that Monday. Six of us, we went out there and had a twelve piece band out there. You know, for a second time I was afraid when I saw that drummer, you know? So when they started playing, and we played at six piece, and I played so much drum there, it took us to play the dance and they sent them out there to play for them kids in the mayor pool. And the fella came to me and said, gee, I wish I could play a drum like you. And I never told him that, the second time I played.
Well you were still a young boy then. Yeah, second time.

And after he told me that, I got bad. I didn't know how to read then. But after you said that, I knew it, the fella told me, he had twelve piece bands, and I wish I had, the fella trumpet player would, you know, right here would die, trumpet player, well they could pass for brothers, just like him. Well they played there. Yeah. And he told me, I wish I had you out here in my band. And I didn't tell him, I said to myself, you didn't know, this is the second job I played. So that's how I went on after that. You said you didn't know how to read then?
Didn't know how to read then. Didn't know how to read.

When did you? Well I'll tell you, when I was playing with Humphrey, you know, Humphrey, well they had plenty of music, and I was playing drumming. Old man Joe Howell said, can you read? I said, no I can't. He said, well you're playing like you can read. I said, no. He said, well you're not, just come to my house. So I used to go to his house when he taught me. Oh yeah, Joe Howell. Yeah. What was he playing then? He used to be a trumpet in his days, young days, but during that time he was playing the tuba. During that time he used to use tuba in the archery. You know that did away with bass, string bass at that time. He used to use tuba. Yeah. So that's how he'd take me and he taught me. Well how did he teach you?
What did he have, how did he teach you? Well he got methods and all that, he understood it, you know. He got methods.

He taught me a little catechism. And I used to have rubber pads, you know, and he used to practice on them. And I went right on like that. Well did he teach you anything about your feet or? Oh yeah, all that. And how to tune up a drum. That's the principle part, tuning up a drum. How do you do that? Well you take like a bass, you tune up that bass, you know. It's like on A. On the A string?
Yeah. On the A string? Yeah.

On the A string? On the A string? Yeah. On the A string? Yeah. On the A string? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You just know if you got a bass there, just tune up that A string and you just bring that bass up until you bring up that A. And it sounds just like that bass.
What about your snare? Do you tune your snare through? Snap through the same way.
You tune the snare drum from the trumpet. Oh, from the trumpet?
Yeah.
Oh. That's why I get such good tone out of my drums like that.
Oh.
Now I can do that by ear now. I can tell now. I don't need that now.
Well, what about those rolls and things? Did you learn that from one jaw?

No, he didn't. Well, the rolls. He didn't know nothing about the rolls. I learned that myself. You just learned that? You see, I learned the music like that while you study. And I learned those rolls myself.
Well, he just teach you like the notes, the…
That's all, yeah, the notes and all that. But the rest of the stuff, I just come to him, I learned myself. A lot of things I pick up.
Well, did you ever have to use that drum music very much? No.

I'll tell you how I used drum music. A lot of the time you play drum music, there's no song like nothing. I'll tell you how I used to use drum, when I was playing in the band in the orchestra. If we get a number and orchestration, they say we're going to play from top to bottom. Well, I look at that introduction there. And I hit that introduction. And I play that twist part. And as soon as I get in the chorus, I use my brain. And I wasn't going in the special like that, but I had to look at that music. And going out, you see. But otherwise, after I played about two or three times, I wouldn't need it. I knew it.
But you had like a quick ear.
